blocks.c: Mike Faist wearing a black suit and striped tie

Rock with Guadagnino and Challengers screenwriter Justin Kuritzkes, but that ultimately fell through. He seems to make decisions, perhaps at the expense of his career, in order to stick to his artistic convictions. The Pulitzer Prize–winning playwright and screenwriter Tony Kushner, who worked with Faist on West Side Story, saw that selectiveness up close. “Two or three people, friends of mine who were making movies after West Side Story came out, called about, ‘What’s Mike Faist like? And Faist delivers a performance so searing that when his character all but disappears at the end of the third episode, his ghost hangs over the rest of the proceedings.

https://media.gq.com/photos/6ab69f92789eaa8545a1848d/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Mike-Faist-Hype-WM-Web-5.jpg

“Look, the truth is, it’s a lot easier for me to put on a character and be in front of the world than be me,” he admits. “And I’m just proud that I’m able to go on a walk with you and do this. For me, that’s a big step."

“Don’t eat dirt,” he says. “You’re worth more. Come on, bub.”

blocks.x: Steinbeck wrote East of Eden as a biblical allegory, alluding to the fall of Adam and Eve and the ruinous brotherhood of Cain and Abel. Unlike her grandfather’s adaptation of the novel, which covered only the last section of the book, Zoe Kazan’s seven-episode series more closely captures the author’s ambitious sprawl.

In the series, Faist is playing against type, taking on Charles Trask, a character introduced by Steinbeck as “to be admired as one admires the sleek lazy danger of a black leopard” and “a dangerous man, even at fifteen.”

Even after Faist expressed interest in East of Eden, Kazan says he needed some persuading to finally commit. “We met twice before he agreed to do this,” she says. “And he was very clear with me, ‘I don’t need you to convince me. I just need to know that this is right for me, because when I jump in, I jump in 100%. If you have me, you’re going to have me 100%.’”

Kazan saw that firsthand on the set of East of Eden. Over the novel’s 602 pages, Charles really figures into only the first 125. In fidelity to the story, Faist was set to star in the first two episodes of the series, with a brief appearance at the top of the third episode. But Faist makes such a forceful impression in the role that after the first dailies of his Charles Trask came in, Netflix was compelled to invest more money into the production.
“Netflix was like, ‘We love him so much. We’ll pay for another episode,’” says Kazan, who found a way to write Faist into a later episode.
In hindsight, Faist thinks he signed on to East of Eden because the work provided a feeling of home, working with a showrunner who also started out in theater.
https://media.gq.com/photos/6ab69f92d714b8297ce424f3/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Mike-Faist-Hype-WM-Web-6.jpg
blocks.c: Mike Faist wearing a black leather jacket and blue jeans

blocks.x: Tank top by Zimmerli. Vintage jeans by Levi's from Raggedy Threads. Belt by Artemas Quibble. Rings by Ten Thousand Things.

“Challengers is the future, East of Eden is a little bit past,” he says. “And I think that, for me, that I had to go back a little bit to basics or a little bit to ‘Why did I get into this in the first place?’”

An analog boy in a TikTok world, Faist often feels like a matinee idol right out of the midcentury. He rhapsodizes about films like All That Jazz, The Bridge on the River Kwai, and Ben-Hur. “You watch that movie and you say, ‘How did they do that?’” he says. “This is magic trick stuff. I’m always kind of looking for that.” One gets the sense that the hot sauce on Hot Ones might literally kill him.

Growing up in Ohio, Faist realized his life’s purpose watching Gene Kelly MGM musicals like An American in Paris and Singin’ in the Rain. “Unfortunately, you can’t go back, but you can bring the past into the future,” he says. (When I ask him what was the last film he felt that for, his answer is a pleasant surprise. “You know what movie I really loved? Passages,” he says, referring to Ira Sachs’s intimate, devastating, terminally horny indie. “Franz [Rogowski]’s performance in that? I’m kind of like, ‘How did he do that?’ So fucking amazing.”)
That reticence to just jump in, the standards he holds for himself and others, seems to safeguard a life that’s more than just a career.
https://media.gq.com/photos/655e31f1d09cc414bca8d206/1:1/w_90%2Cc_limit/GQ_Headshots_RaymondAng_4084-3.jpg

“I think a lot of, especially white, young men who get rewarded really early take it as a confirmation that they’re being anointed and don’t ask themselves deeper questions about it,” says Kazan. “It’s really admirable to me that Mike is pursuing a life that feels authentic to him. And I think that that goes across the board—his relationship to fame, his relationship to his work, his relationship with his family, where he lives, how he lives, his dog.”
https://media.gq.com/photos/6ab69f921fe4ed7af2d684a3/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Mike-Faist-Hype-WM-Web-11.jpg
blocks.c: Mike Faist leaning against a brick building by New Yorks West Side Highway

blocks.x: “Once it’s all over, I’ll go back to construction work,” Faist said in an interview, around the time of his 2017 Tony nomination for Dear Evan Hansen, the Broadway production that served as his initial breakthrough. When I bring up that quote to him now, he laughs and calls it “the narrative of my life.”

“I grew up in Ohio, and my parents—we renovated houses,” Faist says. “That in and of itself is this kind of laborious creative work that I found very satisfying and still continue to find satisfying in ways. And it’s very grounding. It’s real. It’s tangible.”

In 2021, just after West Side Story, Faist packed up his belongings in New York and moved back to Ohio to help care for his ailing father, who was battling pulmonary fibrosis. During that time, father and son renovated a house together—a house he lives in now, whenever he’s not in Brooklyn. His father and grandfather passed within three weeks of each other, right before the release of Challengers changed his life in different ways. “All the men have passed,” he tells me. “It’s my sister, my mom and my grandmother, and me.”

Like anybody who’s left home to pursue their dreams, he feels a push-pull between his life as an in-demand Hollywood actor and his life back home in Ohio. “I’m living in the Matrix,” he says, contrasting the two. “And I’ve got to go back into the real world.”
But in many ways, he’s still just getting started.

Tony Kushner tells me about a screenplay Faist wrote that the actor asked him to look at. “When people do that, you often think, ‘Oh God, help me. It’s not going to be good…,’” Kushner says, laughing. “Then I read it and I thought it was great. He’s also a terrific writer. It’s a very, very interesting, beautifully written script.… He’s very, very smart and empathic and insightful and thoughtful and curious in all the things that you want a writer and an actor to be.”
https://media.gq.com/photos/6ab69f9253df765964c0db31/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Mike-Faist-Hype-WM-Web-9.jpg
blocks.c: Mike Faist leaning against a brick building wearing a black shirt white jeans and sunglasses

blocks.x: Scarf by Charvet. Gloves by Seymoure.

When we meet in August, Faist tells me he’s about to enter rehearsals for the first production he’s worked on since East of Eden two years ago. True to form, he’s tight-lipped about the nature of the production, or even if it is a play, a film, or a TV show.

“There’s things that pop up and for whatever reason, they don’t happen because of the industry and financing,” he explains. “There’s no control in this industry.” Sgt. Rock, for example, was a project he was reportedly attached to last year. “Luca and I remain talking about things from time to time, for sure,” he says now.

“I was so, so excited for that movie,” Justin Kuritzkes says about Sgt. Rock. “None of the people who were planning on doing it were people who were particularly interested in making big superhero movies.… Sgt. Rock was very much a superhero movie that was about everyday heroes, humans, normal people, where the superheroes were really not the focus at all. So it was a pretty experimental thing.” Kuritzkes reveals that they were “more or less in prep” when the film fell apart. (When I ask him why the movie fell apart, he says: “You can ask DC Studios.”)
https://media.gq.com/photos/6ab69f92c55771937824ed8e/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Mike-Faist-Hype-WM-Web-2.jpg
blocks.c: Mike Faist wearing a white suit

blocks.x: Jacket and pants by Officine Générale. Turtleneck by Dolce & Gabbana. Boots by Christian Louboutin. Pocket square by Charvet. Vintage watch by Rolex from Foundwell.
At one point, Faist and I talk about his friendship with Oh, Mary! star and playwright Cole Escola, whom he goes way back with in the theater.
Would he ever consider stepping into the role of Mary Todd? “You know what? I would rock Mary Todd. Why not?” he says.

We live in a different world than the one Faist’s heroes inhabited. We demand a constant performance of intimacy, constant disclosure from our celebrities. In many ways, art is no longer the integral foundation of fame—it’s just another brick in a road made up of memes, TikTok dances, clipped Subway Takes guest spots, and queerbaiting red carpet antics.
In an industry with an increasingly short attention span, with an insatiable demand for product from its artists, will the world continue to wait for Mike Faist?
https://media.gq.com/photos/6ab69f927db5477e046d65ef/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Mike-Faist-Hype-WM-Web-12.jpg
blocks.c: Mike Faist wearing a white suit

blocks.x: “That’s hard with actors, because you can also become an actor who says no to a lot,” Kushner says. “But I’m intrigued by what he’s decided to do and what he has decided not to do and what he’s fought hard to get out of.… I think Mike is a genuinely great actor. That’s not something I say about very many people, because it’s not true of very many people.”

But like some of the actors he aspires to emulate, Faist possesses an essence that has a way of burning through the artifice. In his best work, he seems to be reckoning with the damage wrought by masculinity, the inability to express affection, the cycles of generational trauma. How to be a man. How to be a brother. How to be a friend. And his unknowability—that elusiveness—seems to only fortify what he reveals on the screen. It’s his magic trick.
“I’m always saying,” Faist says, “if you want to get to know me, just watch my movies.”

Passages,” he says, referring to Ira Sachs’s intimate, devastating, terminally horny indie. “Franz [Rogowski]’s performance in that? I’m kind of like, ‘How did he do that?’ So fucking amazing.”)

That reticence to just jump in, the standards he holds for himself and others, seems to safeguard a life that’s more than just a career.

“I think a lot of, especially white, young men who get rewarded really early take it as a confirmation that they’re being anointed and don’t ask themselves deeper questions about it,” says Kazan. “It’s really admirable to me that Mike is pursuing a life that feels authentic to him. And I think that that goes across the board—his relationship to fame, his relationship to his work, his relationship with his family, where he lives, how he lives, his dog.”

“Once it’s all over, I’ll go back to construction work,” Faist said in an interview, around the time of his 2017 Tony nomination for Dear Evan Hansen, the Broadway production that served as his initial breakthrough. When I bring up that quote to him now, he laughs and calls it “the narrative of my life.”

“I grew up in Ohio, and my parents—we renovated houses,” Faist says. “That in and of itself is this kind of laborious creative work that I found very satisfying and still continue to find satisfying in ways. And it’s very grounding. It’s real. It’s tangible.”

In 2021, just after West Side Story, Faist packed up his belongings in New York and moved back to Ohio to help care for his ailing father, who was battling pulmonary fibrosis. During that time, father and son renovated a house together—a house he lives in now, whenever he’s not in Brooklyn. His father and grandfather passed within three weeks of each other, right before the release of Challengers changed his life in different ways. “All the men have passed,” he tells me. “It’s my sister, my mom and my grandmother, and me.”

Like anybody who’s left home to pursue their dreams, he feels a push-pull between his life as an in-demand Hollywood actor and his life back home in Ohio. “I’m living in the Matrix,” he says, contrasting the two. “And I’ve got to go back into the real world.”

But in many ways, he’s still just getting started.

Tony Kushner tells me about a screenplay Faist wrote that the actor asked him to look at. “When people do that, you often think, ‘Oh God, help me. It’s not going to be good…,’” Kushner says, laughing. “Then I read it and I thought it was great. He’s also a terrific writer. It’s a very, very interesting, beautifully written script.… He’s very, very smart and empathic and insightful and thoughtful and curious in all the things that you want a writer and an actor to be.”

Scarf by Charvet. Gloves by Seymoure.

When we meet in August, Faist tells me he’s about to enter rehearsals for the first production he’s worked on since East of Eden two years ago. True to form, he’s tight-lipped about the nature of the production, or even if it is a play, a film, or a TV show.

“There’s things that pop up and for whatever reason, they don’t happen because of the industry and financing,” he explains. “There’s no control in this industry.” Sgt. Rock, for example, was a project he was reportedly attached to last year. “Luca and I remain talking about things from time to time, for sure,” he says now.

“I was so, so excited for that movie,” Justin Kuritzkes says about Sgt. Rock. “None of the people who were planning on doing it were people who were particularly interested in making big superhero movies.… Sgt. Rock was very much a superhero movie that was about everyday heroes, humans, normal people, where the superheroes were really not the focus at all. So it was a pretty experimental thing.” Kuritzkes reveals that they were “more or less in prep” when the film fell apart. (When I ask him why the movie fell apart, he says: “You can ask DC Studios.”)

Jacket and pants by Officine Générale. Turtleneck by Dolce & Gabbana. Boots by Christian Louboutin. Pocket square by Charvet. Vintage watch by Rolex from Foundwell.

At one point, Faist and I talk about his friendship with Oh, Mary! star and playwright Cole Escola, whom he goes way back with in the theater.

Would he ever consider stepping into the role of Mary Todd? “You know what? I would rock Mary Todd. Why not?” he says.

We live in a different world than the one Faist’s heroes inhabited. We demand a constant performance of intimacy, constant disclosure from our celebrities. In many ways, art is no longer the integral foundation of fame—it’s just another brick in a road made up of memes, TikTok dances, clipped Subway Takes guest spots, and queerbaiting red carpet antics.

In an industry with an increasingly short attention span, with an insatiable demand for product from its artists, will the world continue to wait for Mike Faist?

“That’s hard with actors, because you can also become an actor who says no to a lot,” Kushner says. “But I’m intrigued by what he’s decided to do and what he has decided not to do and what he’s fought hard to get out of.… I think Mike is a genuinely great actor. That’s not something I say about very many people, because it’s not true of very many people.”

But like some of the actors he aspires to emulate, Faist possesses an essence that has a way of burning through the artifice. In his best work, he seems to be reckoning with the damage wrought by masculinity, the inability to express affection, the cycles of generational trauma. How to be a man. How to be a brother. How to be a friend. And his unknowability—that elusiveness—seems to only fortify what he reveals on the screen. It’s his magic trick.

“I’m always saying,” Faist says, “if you want to get to know me, just watch my movies.”
